paragraphs.heading: Where rock meets metal
paragraphs.text: The core–mantle boundary, or CMB, is where Earth's silicate mantle meets its liquid iron–nickel outer core, 2,891 km beneath the surface. Seismic waves reveal it: their speeds change abruptly there, because the solid mantle above and the molten core below differ in how they carry sound. P waves slow down sharply in the outer core, and S waves do not pass into the liquid at all.

paragraphs.heading: What the waves tell us
paragraphs.text: S waves work by shearing material, so they cannot travel through a liquid. When they vanish at a depth of about 2,900 km, seismologists conclude that the layer above is solid and the layer below is liquid or molten. The seismologist Beno Gutenberg discovered this break, and it has been called the Gutenberg, Oldham-Gutenberg or Wiechert-Gutenberg discontinuity. Today, though, the name Gutenberg discontinuity more often refers to a different drop in wave speed sometimes seen about 100 km under the oceans.

paragraphs.heading: A rough, hot frontier
paragraphs.text: The uppermost outer core is probably some 500–1,800 K hotter than the mantle resting on it, which creates a thermal boundary layer. The boundary probably has hills and hollows, much like Earth's surface, held up by solid-state convection in the mantle. Seismic tomography shows it is far from even, and that it is dominated by two large low-shear-velocity provinces under Africa and the Pacific. Differences in its thermal properties may change how the iron-rich fluid of the outer core flows, and that flow is ultimately what makes Earth's magnetic field.

paragraphs.heading: The D″ layer
paragraphs.text: Right above the boundary sits a band of lower mantle about 200 km thick called D″, said "D double-prime". The name comes from the geophysicist Keith Bullen, who lettered Earth's layers from A to G, starting with A for the crust and ending with G for the inner core. In his 1942 model the whole lower mantle was layer D. In 1949 he found it was really two layers, so he renamed the upper part, about 1,800 km thick, D′ and the bottom 200 km D″.

paragraphs.heading: Continents at the bottom
paragraphs.text: D″ was later found not to be a perfect sphere. In 1993 Czechowski found that uneven patches in it form structures like continents, called core-continents, which move over time and shape some features of hotspots and mantle convection; later research backed this idea. Recent evidence also hints at a separate layer just above the boundary, possibly made of post-perovskite, a new form of the perovskite minerals found in the deep mantle.
